Four hundred and forty billion euros.

That's how much households in the European Union hold in American technology stocks, according to economists at the European Central Bank.

Most of it doesn't sit in single shares. It sits inside the world ETFs that millions of Europeans buy every month.

At the same time, American stocks trade at their second highest valuation in more than a hundred and fifty years.

That number is the Shiller CAPE: the price of the S and P five hundred divided by its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last ten years. Its long-run average is around seventeen.

The only time they were higher was December 1999. Right before the dot-com crash.

So I took twenty-seven years of real data in euros and replayed what a bubble does to a European investor.

Three rounds of history, one stress test on the portfolios people own today, and ten thousand simulated futures.

Two things surprised me.

First, switching to a safer looking index barely helped in a real crash.

Second, the biggest losses in this replay didn't come from the crash at all. They came from what people did next.

If you own a world ETF, or you put money into one every month, this video is about your money.

By the end, you'll know how many years a bubble can cost you, which portfolios actually held up, and the one decision that cost more than any crash. Let's get into it.

Start with what you actually own.

The most popular index for European ETF investors is the M S C I World.

Over thirteen hundred companies in twenty-three developed countries. On paper, that's the definition of diversified.

European ETFs now hold a record three point nine seven trillion dollars, and this year alone investors added three hundred and eighty one billion more.

But the index is weighted by size. The bigger the company, the more of your money goes into it.

So follow one hundred euros into a world ETF. Every square is one euro.

Seventy-one of them go to American companies.

About twenty-seven go to just ten companies.

If you invest three hundred euros a month, about eighty-one euros of it goes to those ten companies, every single month, without you ever choosing them.

Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Broadcom, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta. Almost every name is an artificial intelligence story.

Nvidia alone is valued at around five point three trillion dollars, more than every listed company in Germany combined.

Put differently, if those ten companies fell by half tomorrow, your world ETF would lose about thirteen percent, even if every other company on Earth stood still.

This concentration is new. Not long ago, the five largest companies were about six percent of the world index.

By the end of 2024 they were close to twenty percent. And the tech sector went from about a tenth of the index to more than a quarter.

None of this is a conspiracy. It's how market cap indices work. When a company grows, you automatically own more of it.

There's no rule that says: this is getting too expensive, let's take some money off the table.

That's exactly why world ETFs did so well over the last decade. You rode the winners all the way up.

But it works in both directions. When a giant falls, it falls with your money inside it.
